evidence: 2 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Record the proving evidence that missing-publisher-data actually drives the alarm to ALARM (e.g. the alarm's TreatMissingData=breaching setting from describe-alarms output, or a drill/history entry showing the transition), not merely that alarms are currently OK.
evidence: AC2: 'the disk alarm re-enters alarm when the publisher dies, instead of self-clearing to OK'
Live close evidence shows only 'Disk-related CloudWatch alarms were OK' with data present
Verification uses 'aws cloudwatch describe-alarms' which shows current config/state, not a demonstrated missing-data transition
findings.finding: AC1/AC2 claim the disk alarms now page on missing publisher data and re-enter alarm when the publisher dies, but the live-close evidence only demonstrates the alarms in OK state with data PRESENT — it does not show a proving observation that missing data actually pages (the specific behavior the incident turned on).
scenarios: A future host-death repeats the original incident because the treat-missing-data-as-breaching config was misconfigured but never actually exercised
findings.suggested_fix: Cite the `describe-alarms` field showing `TreatMissingData` is `breaching` (or `missing`) for rebar-root-disk-pressure and rebar-gerrit-data-disk-high, and/or an alarm-history entry from the incident showing the OK->ALARM behavior on loss of signal.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm the runbook path records the snapshot as the explicit back-out/restore point (reversibility mechanism), not just as a pre-step.
evidence: AC6: 'records snapshot -> modify-volume -> reboot -> cloud-init growpart as an unwedge requiring follow-up reclaim'
modify-volume/reboot on a production Gerrit host is irreversible in-place
findings.finding: The volume-modify unwedge path (snapshot -> modify-volume -> reboot -> cloud-init growpart) is a destructive/irreversible infra operation but AC6 only requires it be documented as an unwedge; no back-out/rollback for a failed grow or the follow-up reclaim ownership is specified.
scenarios: Operator runs the unwedge, growpart fails or reboot doesn't come back, and there is no documented back-out beyond the pre-snapshot

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add evidence that the missing-data alarm actually transitions to ALARM on loss of signal (e.g. show the treatMissingData=breaching config on the named alarms, or a documented test/simulation where the publisher stopped and the alarm paged) rather than only citing a steady-state OK snapshot.
evidence: AC2: 'the disk alarm re-enters alarm when the publisher dies, instead of self-clearing to OK'
Verification: 'aws cloudwatch describe-alarms ... Disk-related CloudWatch alarms were OK' — observes OK state only, not a loss-of-signal breach
findings.finding: AC1/AC2 claim the disk alarms now page on missing publisher data (re-enter alarm when the host dies) rather than self-clearing to OK, but the cited verification only observes current steady-state 'OK' alarm states via describe-alarms — it does not demonstrate the missing-data->breaching transition actually fires. The core behavioral change is asserted, not exercised.
scenarios: A future publisher outage: if treatMissingData was mis-set, the alarm still silently clears to OK and the fix never actually protected the incident it was built for.
findings.suggested_fix: Quote the CloudWatch alarm `TreatMissingData: breaching` (or `missing`) attribute from `describe-alarms` output for rebar-root-disk-pressure and rebar-gerrit-data-disk-high, or record a controlled missing-data test showing the alarm entered ALARM.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the sum of the per-generator root ceilings (Docker/BuildKit + journald + /var/tmp + writable-layer bounds) is provably below root capacity, or explain why the aggregate-worst-case cannot fill root now that gate-scratch is off-volume.
evidence: AC4: 'root usage has bounded ceilings, not merely faster reclaim: the per-generator cap/alarm architecture above is landed and live'
Live close shows point-in-time usage well below caps, but a point-in-time snapshot does not demonstrate the worst-case aggregate of all caps stays below the 60G root
ABSENCE: no statement that sum(per-generator caps) < root capacity, which is what makes per-generator caps a true ceiling on root fill
findings.finding: The per-generator cap architecture bounds each consumer individually, but the plan never establishes that the SUM of per-generator ceilings is below root capacity — so simultaneous peaks of Docker cache + journald + /var/tmp + writable layers could still aggregate to fill root even with every individual cap honored.
scenarios: Docker Build Cache near its 5GiB cap AND journald near its storage cap AND /var/tmp and writable layers near their bounds simultaneously during a heavy merge/deploy burst
